learning_objective: 🎯 Put it all together! Learn how to combine Pandas, SQL, and Matplotlib to plan, code, and document a complete, real-world software project.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Professional software isn't just coded randomly. It follows phases: 1. Requirement Gathering (what do we need?), 2. Analysis & Design (planning), 3. Implementation (coding), 4. Testing (finding bugs), 5. Deployment (launching).
Before writing a single line of code, you must clearly define the problem. For example, 'Our school library loses track of books.' The solution is a Python-based Library Management System.

This is where you plan the architecture. You decide that Pandas will handle the data analysis, Matplotlib will draw charts of popular books, and a CSV file or SQL database will permanently store the records.
Writing the actual Python code. Debugging is the critical process of finding and fixing errors (bugs) so the program doesn't crash when a user types in wrong data.
Code without instructions is useless. Documentation involves writing comments inside the code and creating a user manual so that someone else knows exactly how to install and use your software.

fun_activity.title: 💡 The Startup Pitch
fun_activity.instructions: Look around your classroom or community. Brainstorm one real problem that could be solved with a simple Python script and a CSV file (e.g., tracking canteen expenses, managing sports equipment). Write a 3-sentence 'Startup Pitch' for your software!

exam_tips: 📌 In viva-voce, examiners frequently ask about your specific project's SDLC. Be ready to explain *how* you gathered requirements and *how* you tested it.
📌 Never underestimate documentation. In a practical file, your code comments and clear variable names carry heavy weightage.
📌 Be prepared to explain why you chose a specific technology (e.g., 'I chose CSV over SQL because the data size was small and it didn't require a separate database server').
quick_recap: ⭐ Writing the code (Implementation) is actually just one small part of the entire software development process.
⭐ Testing should always involve throwing 'bad' data at your program to see if it handles errors gracefully.
⭐ A well-documented project allows other developers to easily pick up where you left off.
